European ground squirrels (Spermophilus citellus) exhibit a life history strategy typical of hibernating sciurids, with a relatively compressed active season that constrains reproduction. Gestation in this species lasts for an average of 27 days [tg = 27 days] when core body temperature is maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a period during which the developing embryos are entirely dependent on maternal thermoregulation. Females produce a single litter per year, with a litter size of six pups [N_R_i = a litter size of six pups], a reproductive output that positions them intermediate among European ground-dwelling squirrels. This annual litter [F_R_i = annual litter] reflects the constraints of a short growing season in central and southeastern European steppe and meadow habitats, where females must accumulate sufficient fat reserves during spring to support both gestation and early lactation before the summer dry period.

Neonatal body mass at birth in Spermophilus citellus is remarkably modest, with newborns weighing approximately 5.25 grams [Wwb = approximately 5.25 grams] upon live birth, a value consistent with the altricial developmental pattern characteristic of the genus. These altricial neonates are born fully dependent on maternal care, with eyes closed and limited locomotor ability. Growth proceeds rapidly under the thermal regime maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] within the natal burrow, where the mother provisions the pups with lipid-rich milk. By 30 days since birth, the wet weight of a developing juvenile reaches 61.4 grams , representing a more than tenfold increase in mass from the neonatal stage and underscoring the efficiency of maternal resource transfer during the early suckling phase.

The weaning process, marking the transition from milk to solid food, typically concludes at 34 days since birth [tx = 34 days since birth] when core body temperature is maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. At this point, the young squirrels begin to forage independently on grasses, seeds, and invertebrates, although some maternal provisioning may persist for an additional one to three weeks. This relatively early nutritional emancipation compared to other small mammals of similar body size reflects the selective pressure for juveniles to accumulate sufficient fat reserves before their first hibernation. Field observations confirm that completed weaning in this species spans between six and seven weeks [tx = between six and seven weeks] in free-living populations, with the exact timing modulated by local food availability and the mother's body condition.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs at approximately 314 days since birth [tp = approximately 314 days since birth] under the standard thermal regime of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], which effectively means that individuals born in the spring reach puberty by the following spring's emergence from hibernation. This timing ensures that first reproduction is synchronized with the brief optimal growing season. The adult body mass ultimately attained differs markedly between the sexes, reflecting divergent selective pressures on male and female body size. Females reach a maximum wet weight of 353 grams [Wwi = 353 grams], whereas males achieve a larger asymptotic mass of 380 grams [Wwi = 380 grams], a sexual size dimorphism characteristic of polygynous or promiscuous ground squirrel systems where larger males gain competitive advantages during territorial disputes.

Longevity data for the European ground squirrel, based on long-term field studies in the Czech Republic and Hungary, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 6.7 years [am = approximately 6.7 years] when measured under typical free-living conditions at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] during the active season. This translates to roughly 2,446 days [am = roughly 2,446 days] from birth to natural mortality, a relatively extended lifespan for a rodent of this body size and one that aligns with the slow life-history pace observed in hibernating at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] mammals. The mortality risk is highest during the first hibernation period, after which annual survival stabilizes at moderate levels for breeding adults. Comparative physiological data suggest this species' longevity is intermediate between smaller, shorter-lived ground squirrel species and the larger, longer-lived marmots, reflecting its intermediate body size and facultative social structure.
